nameStory: The water hyacinth gets its name from its gorgeous purple-blue flowers that resemble the sweet-scented hyacinth flowers we grow in gardens. Unlike its terrestrial namesake, this plant has adapted to float on water surfaces, earning the 'water' part of its name.
description: Common water hyacinth is a floating aquatic plant with glossy, thick leaves and showy purple-blue flower spikes. The plant forms dense mats on the water surface, with leaves arranged in rosettes that can spread 1-2 feet across. Its most striking feature is the tall flower spike that rises 4-8 inches above the water, crowned with tubular flowers that have six petals each.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Striking purple-blue flowers arranged in a tall spike, each flower tubular with six petals and a distinctive yellow spot on the upper petal that looks like a peacock's eye

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, glossy, rounded leaves that feel waxy and rubbery to the touch, arranged in floating rosettes with swollen, spongy leaf stems that act like life jackets

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Free-floating plant that forms dense mats on water surfaces, with feathery black roots dangling beneath like underwater curtains

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Leaf stems are notably inflated and bulbous, feeling soft and squishy like a foam pool noodle - these air-filled chambers keep the plant afloat

habitat: Found in slow-moving or still freshwater bodies like ponds, lakes, and quiet river backwaters in New England. Prefers nutrient-rich water and full sun exposure. Most likely encountered in warmer, protected waters during late summer.

seasonality.spring: Plants may appear in late spring in heated or greenhouse environments, but rarely survive New England's cool spring waters outdoors.
seasonality.summer: Prime growing and blooming season, with purple flower spikes most visible from July through August in warmer water bodies.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline as water temperatures drop, with flowers fading and leaves starting to yellow by early fall.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England's freezing temperatures and will die back completely, though seeds may persist.

funFact: Water hyacinth is known as the 'terror of Bengal' because it can double its population in just two weeks under ideal conditions - a single plant can produce 65,000 offspring in one season!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with pickerelweed, but pickerelweed has heart-shaped leaves and blue flowers in dense spikes, while water hyacinth has rounded, thick leaves with distinct inflated stems. Memory trick: hyacinth leaves are 'husky' (thick and rounded), pickerelweed leaves are heart-shaped.
contextualKnowledge: Though beautiful, water hyacinth is considered one of the world's worst invasive aquatic weeds and is prohibited in many states. In New England's climate, it's more of a rare escape from water gardens that doesn't typically survive winters, but climate change may alter this pattern.
compareHints: Unlike its genus relative pickerelweed, water hyacinth is free-floating with inflated leaf stems and rounded leaves, while pickerelweed is rooted with heart-shaped leaves. Water hyacinth flowers are more tubular and ornate with the distinctive yellow eye-spot, whereas pickerelweed has simpler blue flower spikes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pickerelweed differs from its tropical relative, common water hyacinth, by growing rooted in mud rather than floating freely.
